utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Before we deal with the documents tendered through Witness DP2 and the still remaining videotape and transcript tendered through Witness Indic, I'd first like to inform the parties that two decisions have been signed this morning. And therefore, I take it that they have been filed. The first one is the decision on the request for certificate of appeal on the -- to put it briefly, to the decision of the Chamber in respect of the accused -- accused's testimony. The second decision is a decision we should deal with in closed session, or at least in private session. So could we please turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is another issue that I would briefly like to deal with, and that is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I interpose briefly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We're having problems with the connection to LiveNote. Could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you're not the only one, because as you may see, that Judge Nieto-Navia and I am -- are sharing at this moment our portable screen, because we had some difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have none to share. I wonder --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's no -- then we really have a problem, because the Chamber decided that if we would have no access to the -- to the LiveNote, that we could not start. But by sharing it, we thought we could. But if this cannot be solved --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just wait and see what the technicians can do for us. Would the Prosecution agree that I address the other issue even without the LiveNote functioning? Because you might not need that for what I'm going to say now. I do understand that there are at least some problems in respect of the time of arrival of expert witnesses. I was informed that the -- that the Victims and Witnesses Unit was a bit concerned about early arrival and expert witnesses having to stay for a very long time before giving their testimony. The Chamber has instructed the -- one of the legal officers to deal with that, and the Defence should be prepared for a meeting on short notice in order to further discuss the time of arrival of expert witnesses. They should arrive early enough to make the final preparations for their examination and not so early that they are spending, at high costs, a long time without being examined in this court in The Hague. Then while the technician is trying to solve the problem for the Prosecution, Ms. Pilipovic, I think that -- well, perhaps we first should go through the documents. That's an issue which might not cause you to look back in the transcript that much, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at some stage may I address you just for a few minutes in relation to a fresh issue. I don't require LiveNote to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps let's then do that first.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, last Monday, pursuant to a direction from the Trial Chamber, the Defence provided us with the order of expert witnesses that they would be calling. We did not receive until last Friday their list of witnesses for this week. That list indicated the sequence of experts to be, the first expert, Professor Cavoski; the second expert to be Milan Kunjadic, the third Professor Dusan Dunjic. This afternoon we receive a letter from the Defence at one o'clock informing us that instead of expert Dr. Kuljic, the Defence would instead call on Friday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said instead of which witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Who was not previously, in any event, on the list for this week. Dr. Vilicic for Friday, that is, this Friday. Going back to the sequence of the witnesses in terms of their calling, Dr. Vilicic was to have been the sixth witness and Dr. Kuljic was to have been the second. But in the list we received on Friday, Dr. Kuljic did not appear. Instead, Milan Kunjadic and Professor Dunjic. The end result, Mr. President, is something of a mess. The Prosecution is not ideally placed to cross-examine Dr. Vilicic at such short notice. One anticipates that if the order had been adhered to, he would not have been called until either the end of next week or early the week after. Instead, it's proposed to call him in three days. So, Mr. President, I'd be grateful if that order could be reverted back to the original order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will deal with it. But I now better understand why the Defence has indicated the arrival of the expert witness Dr. Vilicic for next Thursday, whereas the Chamber still could expect Dr. Vilicic to testify approximately Thursday one week after that. So this is a surprise for the Chamber as well. We have to consider whether Dr. Vilicic could testify next Friday, because also the Chamber has to prepare for the examination of the expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I just have to say that Dr. Blagoje Kuljic, we had to move him for next week, bearing in mind your position that from the moment when his expert report was disclosed, we needed 30 days to pass. So we expect our learned colleagues to tell us what that time period is. So, Your Honour, that's what you told the Defence yesterday in relation to Dr. Blagoje Kuljic. But I have to say that at this very moment the Defence is in a situation to bring two other witnesses who have been sitting here since last Thursday. And bearing in mind yesterday, because this was unplanned that we should spend the whole day examining Witness DP2, that's why we're having these problems with the order of the witnesses. So now for factual witnesses, the Defence still has a witness today and tomorrow, Mr. Sasa Knezevic and Mr. Sinisa Krsman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So according to the order of the Defence, it will be tomorrow. That's why we've had these problems. It's because of this, that on Thursday we would have Dr. Kosta Cavoski then Mr. Milan Kunjadic then Mr. Dusan Dunjic. But in any case, according to the Defence, Mr. Vilicic would come to testify, but that would depend how long my learned colleagues would be needing to cross-examine our witnesses. Otherwise, Mr. Vilicic would come and testify on Monday. But that's the problem for the Defence. We find it very difficult to plan, bearing in mind the that the Prosecution doesn't use its time in cross-examining the witnesses that it has and that's why it makes all the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. problems for us, calling the witnesses on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Prosecution has filed, meanwhile, their proposals for the time they would need to cross-examine your expert witnesses. And I think if you would follow the order indicated before, that the examination of Dr. Vilicic would not start any earlier than the second half of next week. But we still have to consider whether all the time will be granted. The Chamber is also confronted with a request of the Defence to grant more time for another expert witness. So we'll deal with that on shortest notice. But I do understand that Dr. Vilicic will not be examined by next Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the interest of saving time, perhaps if my learned colleague wishes to change the order, if she could speak to us. Perhaps we can work out some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- Mutually acceptable revised list. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that could be done, the Chamber would welcome the outcome of such a -- such communications. Then is the -- yes, Ms. Pilipovic. Let me first ask whether -- no, the technician is still not ready yet. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I accept that the Prosecution Defence should meet, but I also have to say that the Defence has been informed that the witness who has been summoned by the Trial Chamber - that's Mr. Richard Gray - is supposed to arrive on Sunday. So the Defence is planning that he should be examined on the 12th and the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that should present no problem to us. And I'm grateful for that warning. And if the Defence receives any further warning in relation to other witnesses, I'd be grateful to be informed as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least, the Chamber is glad that the Witness Gray can appear at short notice and that the Defence can examine the witnesses they want to call. So if the parties would sit together and see what schedule they could work out. And the Chamber would really like to be informed as soon as there's any agreement, because the Chamber also has to prepare, especially for the expert witnesses, where we should read the reports, try to understand them, and see whether we have any questions for these experts. Then -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In order to be perfectly loyal, Mr. President, I have had a series of meetings with the possible future witness Mr. Gray, who said that he's going to bring us some material that we haven't seen yet. So I'm saying this now. This is the material that we haven't been able to disclose to the Prosecution because we haven't seen it. We've never had it in our possession. So it -- what I'm saying is there could be some material, some video material, and I will need a little bit of time to view it. And as soon as I've done it, I'm going to communicate it immediately to the Prosecution. So the Prosecution has been forewarned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps we can look forward as well disturb since my learned colleague has already spoken to Mr. Gray, to an updated 65 ter summary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber is aware, since it was involved in the efforts in order to make the witness arrive in The Hague, the Chamber unexpectedly then took notice that spontaneously some offer was made that there might be additional material. So the Defence will have time to look at it and should disclose it as soon as possible to the -- to the Prosecution. At the same time, if it is in the position to update the 65 ter summary of the witness, it should also be disclosed immediately to the Prosecution. Having dealt with the procedural issues, Madam Registrar, could you please guide us through the documents -- the documents introduced through the Witness DP2.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1816, pseudonym sheet under seal; Exhibit D1817, map marked by witness; Exhibit D1818, official note, Sarajevo Romanija Corps, sector of CB for security, strictly confidential, date 9 June 1994; D1818.1, English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having heard no objections, these --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object to the last exhibit, D1818. I maintain the same objection I made when it was presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it so that I know it's not --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is that the Witness DP2 was not party to that document, and he was shown the document and merely asked whether he was subject to the same treatment which is referred to in this particular document. There was -- Witness DP2 was not a party to that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from the document you just mentioned, that is, D1818, the other documents are admitted into evidence and the decision will follow on D1818. Madam Registrar, then we still have a remaining video and transcript that has been tendered through Witness Indic. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we have to say that you didn't want to hear us in relation to this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To what exhibit? The last one? Yes. I do understand that you want to respond to the objection of the Prosecution. You're entitled to respond, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am just going to check which exhibit this is, because sometimes if I have to respond, I might have to do it in private session. So I might have to respond later on if this is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that there was already some exchange of argument. But if you would like to add something to that, you're perfectly free to do so. And just indicate when you find a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can do it now. And I can do it without disclosing anything whatsoever, Mr. President. I do not see why the exhibit D1818 is in relation directly -- it is in relation directly to the person in question if you ask sufficiently elliptical questions, you remember that we did it at the very end of the session and we didn't have to go into a closed session. And that's the reason why I've elliptically asked questions. Otherwise, the exhibit in question does concern the person in question directly. And I don't think it should be excluded, if I understand my learned colleague's intervention. As far as D1818.1 is considered, it's the same one except that it's in English, so that is -- the content is the same, but it has been translated in one of the languages of the Tribunal. Now, if this is not admissible, because it would include somebody else, although I have questioned indirectly, then this objection should not be accepted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Madam Registrar, we'll now move to the video tendered through Witness Indic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The transcript has been given a number by the Defence D184, whereas usually transcripts receive a number with a letter added. So the suggestion to the Defence is to tender the video as D184 and the transcript as D184A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have not fully understood the suggestion of the registrar, so I'll let her speak.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video is D1841. The transcript is D1841A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The matter has been discussed before. And on the basis of the decision of the Chamber that the video could be played, it's now admitted into evidence. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as I am aware of, there are no protective measures sought in respect of this witness, and it would be Knezevic Sasa. Is that correct, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then may the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a technical matter to raise. Following what I just said a moment ago, I do not know whether this kind of exhibits should be tendered under seal or not. I'm asking about the future, in view of the explanation which I just gave you. I am referring to Exhibit 1818 and 1818.1. I don't know if I've made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is not quite clear to me: These exhibits were dealt with in open court, were they not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I now see better. It's because of the content of the document, and I think they will not be put on the ELMO. They -- yes, they should be -- if they would be admitted, they would have to be admitted under seal, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Knezevic, I presume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And the text of this declaration will be handed out to you now by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Knezevic. You will first be examined by counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Before I start asking you questions, will you please give us your full name, your place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Sasa Knezevic. I was born on the 21st of November,--

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Will you slow down because of the interpreters. Will you please go as slow as possible.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: So I was born on the 21st of November, 1971 in Sarajevo, municipality of Centar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in 1992 where were you living at the time and what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I was living in Panjina Kula number 146 in a family house, and I was a student. I was reading world literature at the faculty of philosophy in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, can you tell us, where do you live now and what do you do today?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Now I live at Pale, and I work at the faculty of philosophy as a stated professor for theory of literature and folk literature. That is my subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, you told us that in 1992 you had been living in Sarajevo, municipality of Centar, Panjina [Realtime transcript read in error "Bajna"] Kula Street number 146 and that that was your family house. Can you tell us, at the time -- and I'm referring you to 1992, 1993, 1994 -- whether you also lived at that address. But I will first make an intervention. It is Panjina Kula, not Bajna Kula.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Panjina Kula, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is it all right? I can see it says Bajna --

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, never mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So tell us, that 1992, 1993, 1994, where did you live at that time?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: From 1992 until 1993, I was living in Radava, which is at my grandmother's. And in 1993, I went to Novi Sad, to the university there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So to make it quite precise, when you say 1992 that you were living in Radava, when did you start living in Radava? I'm talking about 1992.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We left the family house in May 1992. And then until September 1993 I lived in Radava.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, when you say that between May 1992 until -- that from May 1992 you have been living in Radava, does that mean that you left your house? If you did, will you give us the reason and when was that in May?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Like this: We left our house because, you see -- now, how shall I put it? We were told that it would be better to leave it for our safety's sake. It was our neighbours who told us. Even, of course, that is questionable, isn't it? But until May 1992 we shared guards with them. That is, in April and may we were out on joint guards with our Muslim neighbours. However, in May they said that we would no longer be safe there and we left our house.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you left your houses, whom do you mean? Your family or ...?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: All Serbs living -- well, there in our small community, you know, left their houses then. There were five family houses that belonged to my Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. family, to the Knezevics.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: We shall come back to that problem later and also to your answer with regard to your houses. Now, will you tell us, since you told us that until September 1993 you lived in Radava, did you -- between September 1992 and September 1993 - and you tell us that that was the time when you lived in that area - were you militarily engaged?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, until September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that you were militarily involved until September 1993, can you tell us from when were you militarily engaged and where?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: After we left our houses, I went first to Montenegro and Serbia, trying to continue my studies. However, I failed to do that because -- because I had not brought my documents and I they had stayed behind at the faculty of philosophy in Sarajevo -- I mean documents from my secondary school. So that I did not manage to enrol in studies and I had to undergo admission tests in Montenegro and in the meantime my father was killed and then I returned to Radava.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you returned to Radava, but you did not answer my question. Where were you militarily engaged?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've forgotten the question. My apologies. Then I was involved with the Kosevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say you were involved with the Kosevo Brigade, that you were a member of the Kosevo Brigade, will you tell us, what were your assignments? And which formation in the Kosevo Brigade did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I started in an infantry unit, but later on -- well, say, in September I was issued with an 82-millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you were issued with an 82-millimetre mortar, can you tell us what positions did you hold and in terms of formation as a soldier issued with an 82-millimetre mortar, who did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: We were on the position in the area of Poljine and it was a battalion. It was, I think -- I think it was responsible for everything that was not the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that it was a battalion and that it was responsible for all that was not the front line, if I got your meaning, can you tell us in relation to the front line, how far were you from it and how many of you were there in the area of Poljine? I mean, persons issued with mortars.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The closest we were to the front line was less than 1 kilometre, perhaps even less than that. And we were six who were responsible for those mortars. In shifts, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Before I continue asking you questions related to your combat orders, tell us, did you serve in the Yugoslav People's Army and what were you --

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I served my military service. I was an infantry man. And I served in Trebinje and Kupari on the eve of the war, that was 1990/1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you told us that the positions -- that your position as a person who was responsible for the 82-millimetre mortar was -- tell us, if you know, your formation. You said a battalion in the Kosevo Brigade. Can you tell us, what kind of a brigade was it and how many weapons and what weapons did the brigade have, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Kosevo Brigade, at least whilst I was there, was not up to the military standards. That is, it was -- did not exist in its full strength. It was a brigade made of people living in that area at that moment, that is, people who had their houses there and people who had fled from Sarajevo, that is, from the part that was controlled by Muslims at that moment. So that presumably it -- there could be five to six hundred men altogether in the brigade. The brigade was a light infantry brigade, so it was infantry. There were mortars. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "I don't know," does that mean that you do not know if there were any other weapons apart from the infantry ones? Or when you say "I don't know," does it mean that there weren't any other? Could you clarify this, since you said it was a light infantry brigade.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I do not know whether there were any other weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the position that you tell us was the position at Poljine, can you tell us if that was precisely the place where you were, Poljine, or is it a wider area? If not, tell us, what is it? What area is it?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Poljine is a wide area. More precisely, the place was called Pretrzanj [Realtime transcript read in error "Pretzanje"], as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Can I just ask that the name of the place be spelled out, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please spell out the name you just mentioned, Mr. Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is spelled correctly. Yes, it was translated correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I also see that it is spelled as you said it, except that an "R" is missing between "T" and "Z."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, since you told us that you were issued with an 82-millimetre mortar, at that place, at that position where you were, were there any other mortars? And if yes, how many? And how many persons were in charge of them there?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: There were three mortars and six men handling those mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say three mortars, six men, can you tell us how many men -- do you know how many men usually operated mortars under military regulations?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, under military regulations of the Yugoslav People's Army, there should be four men per mortar. However, even under these regulations, under certain circumstances, it can be two. So in theory, it is four, but in practice you can never have the number of people presumed by the theory.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Since you told us that you were militarily engaged until 1993, that is, until September 1993, to make it all quite clear, can you tell us if throughout your military engagement, you were responsible for the 82 mortar and were you on the same positions all the time or, rather, on that one position?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Between September 1992 and September 1993, yes. And we always were at that position. We did not change the position.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that in September 1993, if I understood you properly, you left that position, did you -- were you engaged militarily elsewhere? For instance, until August 1994? Or did your military engagement stop? And if it did, why?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: In September 1993, the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska took the decision pursuant to which all those who had enrolled in some university, regardless of where, were exempt, were relieved of their military obligation provided they supplied every year some proof that they had enrolled the next course. So between 1993 and 1998, I was a regular student and I was not militarily engaged anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska had given its consent, did you personally need the consent, the authorisation, of your superior? And if yes, who was that? Who was your superior? That is, who did you get the authorisation to leave your unit?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: That authorisation was signed by the brigade commander, and I had also the authorisation signed by the then-brigade commander, Mr. Miro or Miroslav, I'm not quite sure, Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was he your superior whilst you were militarily engaged on the position at Poljine or was it somebody else? And if yes, tell us who was that.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: He was the brigade commander, and the commander of the battalion was Mr. Vlado Medic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that your superior, the battalion commander that you belonged to was Mr. Vlado Medic, are you telling us that he was your superior in relation to the receipt and issue of orders to you as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: We received all our orders from him, always.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that you spent all your time at the position in Poljine, can you tell us whether your mortars - your mortar - and others, do you know if they were used? And if so, when and how often?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The mortars were operational all the time. Now, how often? Well, as the need arose. As the need arose, in case of the action of enemy mortars or in case of a major and more intensive infantry attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So if I've understood you correctly, you opened fire from your mortars when, in relation to you, the mortars of the enemy were in action and because of, as you told us, more intensive attacks on the infantry. First, I want to ask you: How frequent were those attacks on the infantry? And in that situation, what was your role and from which positions did those attacks come from of the enemy?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in 1992, the attacks were quite frequent. It would happen several times a week. You know, there would be some fire. Whether they were frontal attacks, I cannot really say yes or no. And our role was in case of the action of the enemy artillery or enemy mortars, then if we knew the source of that fire, then we'd open fire on them. And in case of an exclusively infantry attack, we opened fire on positions of the enemy infantry, because at that time the front lines had already been formed both in the areas of Poljine and Kromolj and mostly other parts of the front line covered by the Kosevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you told us that you also responded to the action of enemy mortars, did you have any knowledge - and if so how - and what was that knowledge regarding the positions from which the enemy mortars were opening fire on you?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: We had intelligence information that the enemy mortars were acting from the area of Dumace which -- in the area of Kobilja Glava, then from the area of Humsko Brdo, and on the other side, from the area of -- from near the Kosevo Hospital. It would be on one of the terminals of 17 bus was and also from the area of Pod Hrastovi.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, if the Defence showed you a map of the city of Sarajevo, would you be able to mark the area of -- you told us the hospital, Pod Hrastovi and the terminal of line 17 near the Kosevo Hospital where the buses turned? And you told us that was at the turn of bus 17 where the enemy mortars acted from. Can you do that, witness?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I'll try. I believe I can show it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that would be D1842. I think that is the next number. And with your leave, the Defence would --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, on this map would you please mark the place where you lived. And if on the map we can also see the place which you say is the place called Radava. Mr. Knezevic, do you recognise this map that is in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Then I will ask you to first mark the place where you lived.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Shall I use a pencil?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You'll take a black marker. And make a circle. If you can, will you bring the map down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps zoom in so that we can better see the marking of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... If the question could be clarified a little bit more. Where he lived when?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, before he left the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, put number "1."

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So for the record, the witness underneath the word -- could you read out the street where you wrote "01."

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No. Sorry, between Panjina Kula and Grdonj. So sorry, where I've put the new mark, now between the street of Grdonj and Panjina Kula.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, with "1" and a circle the witness has marked the place where he lived in 1992, and that was between the street -- between the mark -- between the street marked Grdonj and Panjina Kula. So between the two lines indicating those two streets.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, would you now mark on this map the place where you tell us where the positions of the mortars of the BH army in relation to the Pod Hrastovi area.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I'll put number "2."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you also make a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So this is the area about which you tell us is the area which was next to the Hrastovi hospital.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, next to the Pod Hrastovi hospital. It says something else here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Since you lived in that area, can you tell us if that was a hospital which also worked in 1992, and do you have any information if it went on working?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: It was a hospital for lung diseases which did work in 1992. But from what we could hear on the Muslim television during the war, that hospital did not work during the war as a hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On this map, we can see apart from this indication number "2" where you say there is a hospital, there is also an indication for a cemetery. Can you tell us, which cemetery is this?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: On the right-hand side, I don't know. This is turned towards Bascarsija. It's part of the city which I didn't know very well. And this cemetery here is in Humka. That's where I live nearby. Well this Humka, that's vertically towards the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you're speaking about the cemetery that you know was in the area of the city where you lived, that's above number 2. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's Humka.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that where the enemy mortars were was also the public transport number 17 line terminal, was that a tram or a bus?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: It was a bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please also mark that position. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You also told us that the territory of Humsko Brdo and Dumace, for you this was also a target which was where the mortars were firing towards you. On this map, could you please mark the area of Hum and the area of Dumace.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: There is Hum hill on this map but Dumace is not because it probably belongs to the municipality of Vogosca, so it's not on the actual map.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact that we know from previous testimony what Hum hill area is, could you please mark on this map -- can you please indicate if you can see this area.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: It's a wider area of Hum hill here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please put a circle around number 4, please.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you've marked on this map the area that -- or the areas that you've told us were the positions from where enemy mortars were active, were firing, can you tell us whether you personally had information or knowledge - and if you have, what were these - whether the enemy forces in this area also had other weapons at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: What I know is that in the area of Zuc, there was an enemy tank. It fired from the area of Zuc. Then there was an enemy tank that was firing from the tunnels that link up Pofalici, that is, the railway station with Kosevo. And there were also -- it's either that tank or another tank -- there was almost some self-propelled vehicles in the area of the engineering and architecture faculties which are in the vicinity of the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a tunnel. Do you mean one tunnel or two tunnels or more tunnels?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were two tunnels. One was operational, so we usually say "the tunnel."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark the tunnel that was operational and for which you say was used for firing.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: It's here, marked as "1," but I will mark it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please just zoom in a bit more to the marked area. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And when you tell us that the area near the faculties -- you said there was a self-propelled vehicle. Can you perhaps clarify this and be more specific. What do you mean by "a self-propelled vehicle"? Can you please describe it.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: A self-propelled vehicle is a vehicle which has a track. It looks like a tank, but it doesn't have a field gun of a large calibre. It has anti-aircraft machine-gun and an anti-aircraft gun, and it could have a base for firing field guns.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe the area -- can you tell us where the area which that you've identified from which these self-propelled vehicles fired.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Under number "6," this is the area that you have marked as being ...?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Next to the faculties.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you have marked these areas, first of all, I'd like you to tell us how frequently in relation to your positions -- and if they are, how frequently were enemy mortars active, firing towards you?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: In the period when I was there, that depended. Sometimes it would be every day, and sometimes there would be seven or ten days without any firing. But you also have to bear in mind that also during that period there were various cease-fires that were signed during which time there was no artillery or mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, in order to have everything clear, I believe that you told us about the area of Dumace that cannot be seen on this map. Can you perhaps explain on the map what is this area. Where would it be in relation to the positions to the north? Where is Dumace located?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: North. North from this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark on the map the direction.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: That would be the direction towards Vogosca. That is going up there. I can put an arrow there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at it again, whether it says anywhere here "Dumace". Mr. Knezevic, can you please --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please zoom on this area, on this area on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, is this the area of Kobilja Glava and the area of Dumace?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the area of Kobilja Glava.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For the record, we should know what the answer is in respect of -- perhaps it is in respect of what we see on the screen, but perhaps that should be described, delineated for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has put an arrow on the map just below the letter "H." Could you explain to us what that arrow exactly indicates.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asked by the Defence counsel which direction this was going in, and I said this was the north. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I've understood you, you've marked the direction of north as the direction where the area of Dumace was.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No. You've asked me where the north is, so I told you where the north is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But in -- according to you, where would the Dumace area be in relation to Kobilja Glava, if you can find it on the map, the words "Kobilja Glava." They're on the map.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: This map -- no. But it would be about here. But I cannot really tell you on this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how far away is Dumace in relation to Kobilja Glava?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, this is the street, Kobilja Glava. This is a whole area that's called Kobilja Glava. And the area of the city is called Kobilja Glava, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the area of Kobilja Glava, is the area that you told us was called Dumace, which is where the enemy mortars were located?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In a wider area of Kobilja Glava, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, if you can, can you please write between the words "Kobilja Glava" and the direction indicated with an arrow with which you have indicated the north, can you please indicate where Dumaca would be, where you would locate Dumace.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: That would be between the street which is going towards Vogosca and Kobilja Glava.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You can write the word "Dumace."

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, you told us when you answered the question about the frequency of the mortar firing from the area as you have indicated being the mortar enemy positions, you told us that this also depended on cease-fires. Can you tell us, in the area of responsibility where you were, the area of responsibility of your brigade, do you have any information how frequently were cease-fires signed and how were they respected? How long were they valid for?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Cease-fires -- cease-fires were signed on a higher level, of course, and usually they would be violated through an infantry fire incident. It was always done by the opposing side. After which, usually we would complain to the observers or UNPROFOR soldiers who were on our territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that usually you would complain to the observers of the United Nations who were on your territory, in relation to the violations of what I've understood have been cease-fires, these violations were done by the enemy -- can you tell us, these United Nations observers, since when were they in the area of Poljine, if they were there? If you can, can you please tell us the time and the exact location.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what the mission was called, whether they were United Nations observers, or monitors, or whether they were UNPROFOR officers. I don't know. They were there since I was there in that area. At first they were there temporarily. That is, they would come. I think they had a wider area; they were accommodated in Rajlovac, I believe. And then they had their permanent quarters there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, when you say that you would deliver protests to them, can you first tell us what was your cooperation with the UN observers.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know -- I don't know what the command's cooperation was. As far as I know, cooperation was good, because on several occasions, on more than one occasions, I was present at these negotiations, at these discussions because I know the English language.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke -- when you were there, because you knew English, as you say, when you were there with the observers, at any time during these discussions, were you ever given a protest in the sense that you, from your positions, were firing on some civilian targets, civilian facilities in the city?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: During the period while I was there in the unit, we never ever received a protest that -- from our positions anything was fired in order to provoke an incident or that these officers would know about, these observers would know about.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that you opened fire once enemy mortars fired towards your positions from the positions that you've marked as being mortar positions of the enemy, can you tell us, how did you know and how frequently did you respond to the fire coming from enemy mortars?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The information that I had about the positions, this was the information that came through intelligence channels, that is, that I would receive the locations that were indicated marked on the map. Of course, I couldn't see anything from anywhere. From those positions, I couldn't see that fire was opened from those positions. I'm sorry, what was the second part of your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: My question was: How did you know?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I told you. I told you that I received intelligence operative information. Somebody else did it. Or from other positions controlled by Serb forces, or it would be the observation service which existed -- the monitoring service which existed in our brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How frequently? How frequently, in your opinion, during this period - that is, from September 1992 - when you say you were in charge of the mortars, until September 1993 -- how frequently was it that it was from your positions there was firing in the direction of the positions? That is, how frequent was the firing from enemy positions, enemy mortar positions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think I've already heard the question, how frequently, quite a few times. However, the main thrust of my objection is perhaps it could be indicated where he said that he was in charge of the mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood that to be not that he was in control but that he was one of the crew in charge of the mortars. Is that a correct understanding, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The witness was a member of the crew in charge of 82-millimetre mortar. That's how I understood the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Understood in this sense, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was issued a mortar, one mortar. And on that position, there were three mortars. So that is the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you answer: How frequently, from your positions, with your mortar, how frequently did you respond to the enemy mortar fire? Can you tell us, in this period from September 1992 until --

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to say here, throughout this period, while I was there, there was the basic order -- the main order was the defence -- the decisive defence. So this was only to be -- there was fire to be done only in situations that was absolutely necessary -- where this was deemed to be absolutely necessary. There was a shortage of ammunition. There was simply not ammunition to even respond every time. For instance, as this would be demanded by military rules. So we didn't even respond every time when there were all kinds of provocations. For instance, if there were information -- if there was information that came from the front line, from the first line or the front that they were being fired on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, because we've heard the answer of the witness, I think that it is time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn until twenty minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If it pleases you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Before we proceed with the examination-in-chief, may I indicate to the Court that the information in respect to one of the Defence witnesses - and that is Mr. Gray - which we received for the first time this morning, has to some degree caused us to have to make some quick adjustments to our preparations, since we hear now that he's going to be coming next week. And we are doing whatever is necessary not to disrupt the proceedings. However, to avoid further difficulties on the Prosecution side, I respectfully ask if it could be indicated to us as soon as it is known the status in respect to the contacts with the three other witnesses that the Defence had asked to be located and subpoenaed, and also as to whether or not they are available, if they will come, and when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Would you please -- perhaps it's better not to communicate this in open court at this very moment, because it's part of the preparation, and since the Chamber -- at least the supporting staff tried to contribute to the results, I'm certain that the Defence will update the Prosecution perhaps during the next break Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. already. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I was about to suggest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But we could have discussions in the next break and see where we go from there. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I indicated on your request, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that a -- the Chamber had given it some thought -- no. Perhaps first I'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the witness has been scheduled for two hours. May I take it that until the next break that if we're able to -- because until now it's a little bit over three quarters of an hour that you've used. So could we try to finish the examination-in-chief and then have a break so that the witness could then be cross-examined by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just asked whether the order of the appearance of the expert witnesses would still be starting with Professor Cavoski then Mr. Kunjadic and then Dunjic? Is that still the order? Yes. Because then the interpreters should be provided with a copy of the report so that they are able to follow it, especially when it becomes complicated. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. To begin with, to answer to your first question, yes, of course you can do that. And now I will move on to the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I would like to go back to what you told us today at the beginning of your testimony. You spoke about the -- about joint guards. You spoke about the fact that in the very beginning, before the war broke out, you had, you told us, joint guards. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like you to tell us in some more detail what it was about. Can you tell us, what were those guards? How were these guards organised? Were there other Serbs who took part in that, or perhaps were there -- perhaps there were some other ethnicities involved, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Objection. Not relevant to the issues before the Court. Certainly not at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer, Mr. President? Perhaps the witness could remove his headset so that we can gain time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm speaking French, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He could see something on the screen. I don't know whether he speaks any French.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether you -- do you speak or understand any French?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then may the screen be changed and -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. President, why is this question relevant? The Prosecution has for a long time been talking to us about the existence of a plan, the objective of which was to eradicate the whole Muslim population from the city of Sarajevo. Not only the plan -- the plan which was very well organised politically and which spoke about the racial partitioning before the conflict. However, if there exist the joint guards, which were multi-racial, multi-ethnic involving Serbs and others, it would be good to know whether there were such joint guards and how did they come to pass, because that denies the existence of any plan called racists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... In this respect. Let's at the same time try to -- to avoid repetitive evidence. During the first hour we heard a lot about the cease-fire was also violated by the other party. Well, that was not for the first time that this evidence was presented. We heard a lot of evidence on people standing guard. But if you would then perhaps specifically deal with the aspects you just mentioned, that's fine. And Mr. Stamp, may I ask you: To some extent the Defence is free to use its time as indicated in the way it deems fit to use its time. At the same time, discussions on relevance sometimes take more time. And as you know, this is not a jury trial, but we are professional Judges. And if sometime some irrelevant aspects would appear, the Chamber would certainly be able to keep an eye on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. As it pleases you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness -- witness, can you see the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it would be good if the witness could see it for purely spelling reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll first wait until the part discussed has disappeared from the screen, and then of course the witness is fully --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, excuse me. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, will you answer this question: What can you tell us about the inter-racial community, that is, the multi-ethnic composition of these guards?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: In early March, after the members of the Serb wedding party were killed, the tension began to mount. Barricades were put up around the city. And in our neighbourhood, a community meeting was held between more prominent Muslims and Serbs, and it was decided that on our street, on Panjina Kula, joint guards should be mounted involving one Muslim -- one Serb and one Muslim. These guards were in effect for about a month, that is, from the beginning of the month of April when -- or rather, until the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was proclaimed. Then the Muslims set up their barricade at the end of this street where they lived ethnically, that is, where only Muslims lived. And in this part where there were mixed people, that is, both Serbs and Muslims, the guards were not organised to patrol. We stood at two points, one Serb and one Muslim, and that was throughout the night for hours. That is, we had two shifts. So these guards now functioned for about ten days, because at that time the fighting was already gaining momentum in other parts of the city. And first we started receiving from Muslims answers, "Well, you know, it's difficult to keep on eye on who's coming here." They simply wanted to say that they were losing control over the type of organisation which existed at the time. So that -- so that in early May, when all these things with the army happened, simply -- although, we were the only ones who were performing control over everything in that area -- first small formations began to come there in cars. In the beginning, they were introducing -- they said that they were reserve police force, but in their area the reserve police force was ethnically pure, that is, Muslim. And we of course complained. We said, "No, you can't do it, that is not our understanding." But they said, "We cannot simply under control any longer." And the situation became impossible for continuing because the Muslims came to our houses and at some point they wanted to start writing down the names of those living in houses and the like, which all told us only one thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Thank you. You told us, witness, also that your neighbours told you to leave, advised you to leave because they -- your safety could not be guaranteed any longer. And you spoke about Knezevic houses. You told us there were five such houses which belonged to the extended Knezevic family. Can you tell us, first, what has become of those houses? And two, when?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: After -- we withdrew, or rather, we moved house some 500 metres away to the -- our neighbour's house, and that is where we were. And after what happened and the attack on Pofalici -- as a matter of fact, from the areas from which the Serbs had withdrawn, as in our case, the houses were burnt down. In our case, fire was put to them, even though there were 15 Serb houses, only the houses of the Knezevic family were put fire to, and I guess that the reason for this was that we were indigenous population, that we've lived in that area for a very long time -- or rather, the wider area in which we lived, used to belong to my family. Until the 1970s, when the state nationalised this land and when they started building other houses on the nationalised land. And we guessed that the Muslims could possibly or presumably think that if they set on fire those houses of those who would be the first to come back, then others would see no reason to stay in that area either.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You are telling us about burnt houses. Can you tell us, how did that happen? Was it by accident? Was it arson? What do you know about that precisely? Some detail.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of June, 1992, from those positions which were relatively near our houses, first our neighbour saw our house in flames and then my relatives' house, which was next to ours, and that was right there. Now, of course, I cannot say who did that; although, of course, I can make some educated guesses. But towards the end of June of that same year, some kind of conversation -- although, I mean -- some people remained captive on the Serb side so that that delegation of Muslims from the street came there for exchange, of course. And among others, there was an acquaintance of ours who then named to my father the person who had set our house on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness -- no, I'm withdrawing what I wanted to say. The person who did that, to your knowledge, was that person from the army, from an armed formation? Or was that a civilian or what?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The person who was named by that other man was a kind of a commander in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: A civilian or military?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: When we say "commander," then we always mean military.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps it would be useful to hear that name, and the Prosecution intends to start perhaps the prosecution of other persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you give us that name? Would you be ready to give us that name if we were protected? Would you give us this name? Would you mind doing that?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Listen, my mother's got enough troubles in Sarajevo with regard to her property.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'm changing the subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's improper to suggest that if the witness mentions a name, that this could result in prosecutions against that person. This would -- this is at the same time asking and at the same time -- at the same time giving reasons for hesitation on the part of the witness, which is not proper to do. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. Thank you. I'll change the subject. No. I'll change the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And I'd like us now to focus, witness, on the protests, or rather, their absence that you mentioned with regard to what my colleague said. You spoke to us about the presence of UN officers, but you did not tell us who were they. I'd like to know how often did you communicate with them, whoever they might be, whether they be military observers or people from the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Personally, I communicated with them on about ten or so occasions. For instance, when they would leave, they would come to say goodbye. And other times when we lodged those protests with them. And for instance, once I communicated with them at the time when we were repairing -- what do you call them? Oh, yes, the transmission lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. When they came and when you met them on those dozen or so occasions that you indicated to us, were you able to see that, for instance, the contact was bad or so because such-and-such protest was not followed upon or I don't know what, or were these contacts always good?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, these contacts, this communication was always very correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like us to go back to what you said a moment ago, and you spoke about an attack on Pofalici. And I'd like you to tell us a little bit more about it, that is, when did this attack take place? Where did it come from? That is, from which area did it come, and what happened? In two words, please.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly what happened. What I know is that in that attack my aunt and my uncle were killed. That is what I know. That Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. attack happened, I suppose, from Donji Pofalici against Gornji Pofalici, where Serbs lived. And a large number of Serbs were killed. Then there were have many wounded. My aunt was wounded, for instance. And she succumbed to those wounds in the hospital. Also, a number of Serb houses were set on fire during that attack. That is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I need something more precise. Your aunt -- or your uncle, were they activity involved with the army, or were they simply civilians? What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: She was a civilian, and my uncle too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. What kind of wounds -- or perhaps what kind of weapons inflicted those wounds? What kind of weapon inflicted those wounds -- inflicted those injuries which -- or, rather, what type of weapons were used to inflict injuries and subsequently the death of your relatives?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I really do not know that. It was only after the war that my relatives managed to exhume first my uncle's body, who had been buried somewhere else, by the cemetery, and then my aunt, who had been buried in the Lav cemetery, which is the cemetery below the clinical centre, that is what I know. I don't know anything about the nature of injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But did they die as a result of war?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, now I'd like us to touch upon the technical matters concerning the weapons. You spoke to us about the opening of fire in response to the fire coming from the other side. Did you have any instructions coming down the chain of command, that is, not to use weapons except to respond to the fire? And if so, did these instructions reach you orally or were they in writing?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that. The chief order was the defence as a last resort, that is, defence only where lives of our men or other people were in serious threat. We -- or rather, I then acted only when receiving an order to do that, and such orders at first arrived orally. In the early days we had a radio station. Later on, telephone communication was established. And from time to time, Mr. Medic issued orders personally. But that was when the situation had deteriorated somewhat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You tell us, witness, that in the early days you were -- you were not -- you were not an artillery man. You were just with the infantry. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you were just a foot soldier, what kind of weapon did you have?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I had a semi-automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And as such, did you also, when you were a simple infantry man, did you receive the instructions concerning your weapon and the opening of fire? In other words, did this come down the chain of command? Were there orders to respond or not to respond in one way or the other? What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the order was to return the fire. And one of the orders, which was a standing order, that is, to which we always had to pay attention to, was that in case of a cease-fire, the conclusion of a cease-fire, not to open fire first but to first say -- or rather, to inform the observers about it. And after they had been told about it and if the situation was really difficult, to only then return the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, to open fire of course involves certain risks. Were there certain instructions issued concerning civilians? That is, concerning the conduct that you were to observe in relation to this problem, the problem of the existence of civilians?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: There was the order never to open fire on civilians. That is, in no case were we to open fire on civilians. While we were on our mortar positions, we had been issued a warning which had to do with the Geneva Convention. I really cannot tell you much about the Geneva Convention as a convention, but we were drawn attention to humane warfare, which excludes any possibility of targeting civilians. That is something that was always present.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I am taking up your answer once again because you are telling me about the time when you were serving, when you were managing the mortar. That is what I read from the transcript. But does your answer also apply to the -- to the previous period, that is, the time when you were still just a plain foot soldier, a plain infantry man? Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Sure. But at that time we didn't have -- didn't have that order in writing, which we later had.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And if I understand well, the distinction is that you had this order in writing at the time when you operated the mortar but this order was merely oral at a time when you were just a foot soldier. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, that is the basic difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And with regard to this oral instruction, would it be to your understanding what at times is called a standing order, that is, a permanent order?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a standing order. But now and then people from the command would come and repeat it to men. I don't know why they did it, but it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I'd like us now to go back to the issue of mortars. You told us that you were issued with an 82-millimetre mortar, that is, that you handled 82-millimetre mortars. What can you tell us, witness, about the mortars used by the adversary forces? And I'm seeking technical precision in that respect.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: According to the shrapnel fragments that we found, they had 60-millimetre mortars and mortars which use 82 or more millimetres. One could not say that -- or rather, it is the same kind of weapon which is used by different armies. For instance, the Yugoslav People's Army used 82-millimetre mortars; others use 81-millimetre mortars. So I cannot really tell you which one of these mortars was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Did you -- on your positions could you there see craters of 120 millimetres, for instance?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No, not from our firing positions. But in Radava, where I lived during the war -- or rather, above Radava was a road which connected Ilidza and Pale, and that area was shelled quite often. So we found there fragments, of course in places where those shells fell. And I saw with my own eyes a whole, unexploded shell, which looked very strange. We did not touch it because we couldn't really understand it. There was a fuse missing, and that was very odd indeed. That is, it simply could not go off.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you here. I have to interrupt you. What I want to know, witness, at the moment is: Craters that you perhaps saw. So my question is: Could you -- did you see craters which in -- on hard soil, say, on concrete or in asphalt or in some -- on some similar surface? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you saw that, with your own eyes, witness, were you able to see if a shell from -- which exploded, could such a shell pierce this hard surface? And I'm talking, for instance, of the whole asphalt layer. I mean, go through it.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: A mortar shell? No. Simply, it explodes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you here. Since you say no, could you please tell me what happens if a shell hitting the surface explodes? Could you give us a brief description of what we can find following the explosion.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The shell explodes. Depending on whether it hit a hard surface or a soft surface, then depending on the angle on which it's fallen. Then there's shrapnel flying around. It depends how the shrapnel will go, how far it will go from the impact. But that's the whole point of a mortar shell, that when a mortar shell explodes, there's as many -- there should be as many pieces of shrapnel as possible because that is a -- this kind of weapon, that the shrapnel would disperse as far away as possible and then obviously hit during that explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. How does a crater appear to an observer who would look at it, who would be observing it? Such a crater, what does it look like?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not a large crater. A shell cannot -- a mortar shell cannot make a large crater. It would be about 30 centimetres probably, and it will be quite shallow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. Thank you. But now, in relation to the depth, the depth of the crater on an asphalt surface, what is the depth of the damage done to the surface?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how thick the asphalt layer is, but it never goes through the asphalt. It doesn't go through the asphalt.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
