utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you know anything about - that happens as a general rule - what happens with the stabiliser, that is, the tail fins of the shell once the shell has exploded?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The stabiliser either ends up where the main crater is, or sometimes even because of the reaction, sometimes it even goes back. It falls off.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you also spoke to us about the problem of ammunition. You told us that you would not be firing very frequently because you were economising ammunition. Do you recall your answer?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. This answer was given by you when you were telling us about mortars, and I'm going to ask you the same question in relation to your career as an infantry soldier, that is, the questions in relation to economising ammunition for infantry soldiers.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The order was always to fire only if the infantry soldier was at risk. So if -- only if you are fired at, then you fire back. In other situations, it was simply not allowed to fire. And people accepted this very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm going to now come back to the question of heavy weapons. You told us about the presence of tanks earlier, and you told us about the presence of a quasi-tank. As far as I've understood, that is, a vehicle that was mounted on a base and that it had a smaller calibre field gun than that of a tank. And my question in relation to this is now to do with weapons that were mobile, that were able to carry mortars. Do you know, while you were --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is introducing an element into evidence of this witness by telling the witness about something which he did not mention when asked quite clearly about it more than once by the other learned colleague for the Defence. That is very, very leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you are, I think, the French word would be almost like a "souffleur" who tells the people on stage what will be their next line. We heard a lot of evidence in this respect, and I think I've warned you several times that since the effects of such leading questions cannot be undone, would you please move to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Very well. I have certainly been carried by the blast of the explosion to be prompting -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, witness, if you knew or if you know about other weapons that you may have forgotten about - and I'm now talking about heavy weapons - I am not mentioning any names - but if you knew that there were other weapons, apart from those mentioned, could you tell us and could you let us know? Not necessarily mobile. Any weapons, heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I forgot to say earlier that again, in the direction of Radava, on that part of the road from the direction of Grdonj, which is very near my house where I was born, there was some weapon that was active. It was probably a recoilless gun. That happened on several occasions in the direction of that road because it was within view range. And then from the same direction on several occasions, what came were these -- there were guided rockets, and it was according to the firing of the mortar from the area around the Kosevo hospital, which would also include the area of those two faculties, the architectural and the engineering faculty, we -- because of where they came from, we assumed that the opposing side had mobile mortars. Now, this assumption or supposition that we had, this was confirmed by the opposing side themselves, because very frequently they spoke about the success of their unit, and they called that unit James. And this unit, in fact, represented or was a vehicle with a mortar mounted on it. It was well known in the army. It wasn't anything special, that is, that mortars of calibre lower than 60 and 82 can be mounted on a vehicle. And you can actually fire them while they're mounted on the vehicle. You don't have to take them off the vehicle except you have to reinforce the actual vehicle. You can do that with larger calibre mortars but then you have to put them -- attach them to vehicle and then you have to tow them. So very frequently the enemy would have to fire and then the firing would change location, so in one hour we would have firing that we couldn't control. That is, it didn't come from the same place. It was very confusing, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, before we go to another subject, another line of questioning, could you tell us whether the name of Seva means anything to you, that is, the Seva group. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. What can you tell us briefly about this group, about the Seva group?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: According to what I know, it's a special unit, a kind of special unit of the Muslim forces. And according to what I know, they fired on us from the maternity building near Kromolj, and this information, we were able to get that from the media, from the Muslim part of Sarajevo. This is not something that they covered up. They boasted of firing from that location onto Serb positions, that is, Chetnik positions as what they called it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you spoke to us about a special unit, how were they special? In what way were they special, these units -- or this unit?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: It was a special unit which, according to what they said, they used snipers to fire. It was a sniper unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, now I'd like to come back to another aspect of our questions. From the position or the positions that you were at, if you moved -- did you have from those positions, did you have an open view of certain parts of the city?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Our positions were in the city. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. However, that is not what I wanted to ask as a question. One can be in the city and still have a view of the city and you can be outside and not have a view or have a view. So for someone who was not inside a trench, did you have a view of the city of the opponent?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. On this part that you had the view, were there any facilities, that is, in terms of buildings, were there any buildings, residential buildings, any monuments that -- any monuments of any symbolic value, historic, cultural, religious, et cetera? For instance, mosques, important monuments, and so on.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in Sarajevo there are lots of mosques, and yes, there was a mosque at Kobilja Glava certainly. And there were mosques in that part of the town -- the city, in the centre, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Did you have a view on the minarets?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever receive an instruction, an order from the military hierarchy, to target or destroy such facilities?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I never received such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if these facilities could have been used by the other side, by the opposing army? And if so, to which -- with which objective?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Of course they could have used them. I don't know whether they did use them. They could have used them perhaps in order to provoke -- to provoke an odium towards the Serbs in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, you spoke to us earlier about an area which we are particularly interested in, and that is the area of the faculty of architecture and engineering faculty, and also the area of the hospital for lung diseases, I believe. You mentioned it earlier. My question is the following: First of all, do you know about other hospitals or other hospital complexes that were in the area; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: In that area was the Kosevo Hospital, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, do you know if in the area of the Kosevo Hospital, generally speaking, there were military operations that went on in that area?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: In the wider area of the hospital --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... To answer. It is yet another leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we just heard an answer of the witness where he said he did not know whether any facility was used by the opposing party. But invited by you, he said how it could have been used. Of course, it certainly could have been used. It's pure speculation you're speaking here. You are leading the witness again. Why not examine the witness in a proper way. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well. Yes, with pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know -- no, I withdraw that. I'll rephrase it. Earlier you spoke to us also about a cemetery that was located in that area. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: There are two cemetaries. There is Humka [Realtime transcript read in error "Humska"] in Pod Hrastovi, and the cemetery Lav near the Kosevo Hospital -- the Kosevo stadium. It's not Humska but Humka. It's a correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Duly noted. Thank you. I asked you a question in relation to this civilian nature and their hypothetical targeting, their targeting, being taken as a target. I don't have the Serb interpretation -- oh, it's coming back now. Yes. Did you have the entire interpretation, sir?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I've had the entire interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I will rephrase. Earlier, I have asked you about civilian facilities in relation to hypothetical targets, that is, that these civilian targets could have been hypothetically targeted -- these civilian facilities could have been targets. That -- we spoke museums, mosques, cultural monuments and so on. And you gave me an answer. Now, I'm going to ask you the same question in relation to cemeteries, cemeteries as such. And secondly, and ceremonies that could have happened. What I mean by "ceremonies," I meant funerals. No, I meant funerals. I meant funerals, burials.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: We never had an order to target cemeteries, nor did we ever fire on cemeteries.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I can remind you that your last question -- in approximately eight lines you reminded the witness of your earlier question and that he answered that question, which is to suggest that this question is similar or the answer would be similar. A proper way of putting that question to the witness was: Were you ever -- did you ever receive orders to fire at ceremonies such as funerals or burials? That would have been the proper way of putting that question, instead of reminding the witness of his earlier answers and saying that the question is a similar one. Please proceed. I'm asking your attention for it, because the way you are putting questions to the witness might diminish even the value of his testimony, and that's the last thing I think the Chamber would --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. I understand you, Mr. President. I thought that in French -- and I asked the question just like you said, and I asked the question like that, as you suggested. I do not think that the Defence will have any more questions, but I have to confer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, is the -- what I wanted to say is the Prosecution ready to start the cross-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed we are, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, you said you met with UNPROFOR or UNMO officers about 10 to 12 times? I am understanding you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, about ten times. You can say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you attend these meetings in the capacity of an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Some, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who normally would be present at these meetings, apart from yourself?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, as the brigade commander, and these officers and their interpreter, if they had this person with them. But if they didn't, that's when I came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many times did you have meetings with the UNPROFOR or UNMO officers in the presence of Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Five or six times. I mean, Miro Krajisnik, just to be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did you at any time ever hear of any protests from the UNMOs? Not necessarily involving your unit, but any protest at all about firing of weapons by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the meetings where Mr. Krajisnik was present. This was to do with the Kosevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you at any of those meetings hear any complaints, protests, or issues raised by the UNPROFOR members in respect to the firing of weapons by the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think the answer was no, but I'm not seeing it on the record. Neither do I hear the interpretation. Perhaps you could answer it a bit louder, please.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What were these five or so meetings in respect to?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I said on several occasions our commander filed a protest, and on two occasions we followed the observers. You understand, they were going back home to their base.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm talking about the five or six times when you met with UNPROFOR or UNMO personnel in the presence of your brigade commander. You're saying that -- well, let me repeat: What were the meetings when Mr. Krajisnik, your brigade commander, was present with the UNPROFOR members about? What were those meetings discussing? What were you discussing - I beg your pardon - at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik called these meetings in order to protest about the firing of the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did UNMO or UNPROFOR personnel ever visit the area or the place where your mortar unit was located?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Their position was nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How far from where your mortar unit was located was their position?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Not further than 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when did they establish -- well, before I say that. I think you could tell me whether I'm correct or not. You said your mortar unit, your squad or battery was in the same position between September 1992 and September 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when did the UNMO or UNPROFOR personnel establish their location, approximately 200 metres away from you?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: That was in the course of the winter. I don't know whether it was 1992 or 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All right. Assuming you left there in September 1993, would it be the winter of -- would it be the winter of 1992, going to 1993?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was winter 1992/1993. That's the winter I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I'm just understanding you now. While you were at that location, and that is where your mortar unit was positioned, could you see into the part of the city which was under the control of the opposing side?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No. The mortars are positioned so that they cannot be seen by the opposing side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you see the mosque at Kobilja Glava?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know if the mosque at Kobilja Glava was destroyed or damaged during the war?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No meaning it was not, or no meaning you don't know?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I said yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Just for the interpretation, what I heard from the witness is that he said "da," which I understand to mean yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could be asked to answer a little more audibly, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please speak a bit louder, because the interpreters have really problems in hearing you. And perhaps, Madam Usher, the microphones could be adjusted in such a way that there would be less problems. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it you mean yes, you knew that it was damaged during the war?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know what caused the damage?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you were at your -- withdrawn. Do you know whether or not it was repeatedly shelled by the VRS between September 1992 to September 1993 and beyond?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said that during your time there was a shortage of ammunition. Was this shortage of ammunition a rare condition or a condition that the unit found itself in right through the one year or so that you were posted with the mortar unit?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't the shortage really, but there was always fear of a major attack during which we'd need large quantities of ammunition and we didn't have those.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All right. In this regard, did you have or did any member of your mortar battery have a responsibility to record the usage of mortar rounds, that is, how many times you fired and what you fired at and whether it was hit? In other words, was there a log kept of your outgoing rounds?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medic kept record at the battalion level. It was the battalion which took care of these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Medic was not with your mortar battery at all times.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Nobody was with the mortar -- in the mortar unit at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So can I take it, therefore, that reports would have to be made to him regularly about the firing of your mortar battery and the use of ammunition?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. And he also ordered to open fire. Of course he was kept informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, these reports that were made about your firing, were these reports made in writing?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you have target lists, and that is lists of certain positions that you could be asked to shell at any time?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I had targets drawn on the map, and then the order would come to open fire on certain targets, rather, the coordinates which we had on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, sometimes these targets were the enemy infantry at their front lines; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Those front lines, can you say how far they were from the VRS front lines? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the lines varied. At places it was 100 metres, at others three, four hundred metres, but that would have been the biggest distance in the area of responsibility of our brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you receive orders to fire at these varied areas of the enemy front line, sometimes the lines at 400 metres, sometimes the lines at 100 metres away? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you also had various targets that you fired at within the city of Sarajevo which you could not see.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: We had targets only where the enemy artillery and infantry were. When you say "inside the city," I don't know what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you -- were the targets that you had drawn on the map and the coordinates that you got in respect to targets in any part of the urban area of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Within the urban area of Sarajevo were also our front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yeah. But did you have any targets on your target list on the maps or on the coordinates which were within the urban areas of Sarajevo? Did you fire into that area at targets?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've shown you the positions of the mortars. For instance, Pod Hrastovi, that is the position of mortars inside the urban area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you receive any orders to fire at what you -- well, what you said you heard were mobile mortars?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. You can't use mortars to target mobile targets, motorised ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Because a mortar projectile from the place it is launched to the place it is targeting, it takes 45 seconds. In 45 seconds, a mortar projectile can cover a very large distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And there would be the possibility or the likelihood that by the time the mortar projectile arrived, that motorised target would have moved on. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it further follows from that, if I understand you correctly, that there would be no military purpose in doing that.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No purpose to target a mobile target from a mortar. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Did your mortar units have spotters or observers or perhaps I should just describe the functions. Did your mortar units have persons, by whatever name they might be called, who were responsible for observing the city to see where your rounds landed, to see if they were on target?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you ever receive a report that your rounds had hit and caused injury to civilians in the city?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Who could I get such a report from?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your observers.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Our observers were on our side. And whether we saw that some target had been hit, no. And we never targeted civilians. How could we hit them?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand you're saying you never targeted civilians. When you say "how could we hit them," you mean you could not hit them because you never targeted them?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we never fired at civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How about in the area of your front lines? Did you at any time hit your own troops by mistake, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think it ever happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During your tenure --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think the witness is indicating he's having problems with something.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The interpretation wasn't getting it. I said it never happened to me. And the interpretation is "I don't think," which means that the interpretation is not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks for the clarification, witness. During --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's -- if there's any reason to assume that the interpretation is not correct, you may address me, and we'll seek to clarify the issue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During the time that you spent with your mortar unit -- withdrawn. May I ask: You said earlier that at first you communicated with your command by radio and later by telephone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by RUP 33, which is an army radio station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And later on by telephone. Was that a wireless telephone or a wire telephone?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Our signalman had connected the trenches and the rear, the artillery by wired telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you communicate with your battalion headquarters or with the brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: We received our orders only from the battalion command or the brigade, depending on where they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, if you would find a suitable moment for a break soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we go, one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know whether your battalion headquarters or your brigade headquarters had the facility to communicate directly with the corps headquarters in Lukavica? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then adjourn until five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, since you're on your feet, I take it you want to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, the Prosecution and Defence and Ms. Tournaye met during the break -- in fact, for the duration of the break to -- in order to work out the sequence of witnesses. We've succeeded in agreeing to the sequence of witnesses for the balance of this week and for Monday next week. Tuesday is a holiday. We've been unable to determine the witnesses for Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday. Presumably Mr. Gray will be in there somewhere. I'm informed that the Defence cannot further discuss it tomorrow, not available because of other commitments, which means that we're now looking at Thursday before we know the identity of the witnesses next week. And again, we should have been informed yesterday or last Friday of the witnesses for next week, given the seven-day rule. So, Mr. President, that's the situation. We do need to know who will be called next week. So I'd be grateful for a direction to that effect, to ensure that result. I think it was helpful that the three parties met and talked about it. But we do need to meet. Perhaps if the parties were required to meet during the first session tomorrow, then we could make some more progress then. But even then, it's mid-the week before, before we know who the witnesses are for the following week. And these are significant witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I do understand that it's your intention to continue the meeting as soon as possible. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, nobody's perfect. The Defence did not say that they would not agree to a meeting tomorrow. What they say: If there is a meeting, then it will be without me, which is not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I do understand that there is a possibility to meet tomorrow. At what time, Ms. Pilipovic -- because I do understand that it is you who would have to meet with the Prosecution. At what time could you do that?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, 1300 or perhaps half past 12.00. We can meet then with our learned friends. But I'd like to indicate immediately in view of the information that we have received from your associates, Mr. Dunjic should be arriving on Monday, because Thursday and Friday were planned for Mr. Kunjadic. I need to say straight away that the Defence has heard from Mrs. Guskova, who was scheduled for Monday, but I think it really did not depend on Defence that things changed, that the schedule was upset. She can arrive on Saturday and she can only be available now on Monday. Now, I can talk to the doctor, if he's return to tomorrow, according to the information, and then to come back on Sunday to be available on Monday. So this is the information which perhaps we could clear up with our learned friends tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, the Chamber is not available at this very moment to say exactly how the problem can be solved and who has what kind of obligations to fulfil. And therefore, I think as far as the content is concerned, the Chamber at this moment could not greatly assist you. But I would say that the meeting, as far as I understand, your discussions could not be finished. Would tomorrow at 1.00 be suitable?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand from Ms. Tournaye and there is already a meeting booked with the Defence and Ms. Tournaye and I think the witness unit. She suggested 12.30, and so I also suggest 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would have one moment of patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn presumably for not more than one or two minutes. --- Break taken at 6.16 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber was concerned about when the parties could continue its meeting and try to find out when Ms. Tournaye would be available. Unfortunately, we're not able to -- to establish when she would be available. May I ask the parties to make themselves available for further -- yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: An alternative suggestion, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Since she is meeting with the Defence and the witness unit tomorrow at 1.00, perhaps we could be informed just before the session commences tomorrow afternoon if there has been some further progress on that. It may well be that the order will be settled at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would it be of any use to have a short meeting just prior to that meeting with the Victims and Witnesses Unit? So let's say at -- if the meeting would be at 1.00, then to meet at 12.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes? Okay. Then we'll see whether Ms. Tournaye is available at 12.30 and not only at 1.00 and see whether any progress can be made then. Then if there's nothing else, the witness may be brought into the courtroom. And please, Mr. Stamp, proceed with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You mentioned where some enemy positions and enemy military assets, enemy heavy guns were located. Did you actually see these positions or these heavy guns at these locations, or were these intelligence reports that you received?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: It was from intelligence sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And apart from those locations which were marked on a map, were you at other times given the coordination -- or the coordinates for any other locations to fire at?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No, except the enemy trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At the time you fired, is it correct that you would not know exactly what was present or happening in the target location?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I had information that those were military targets. Whether an enemy mortar unit or the enemy front line, well, now, it varied from one case to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you did not know that -- this personally when you fired this was information that you had.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In other words -- all right. Let me ask you. What would be the point of repeatedly telling your mortar unit not to fire at civilians where you could not see the place that you were targeting?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: From the mortar position, you can never see the place you are firing at. It is done upon orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In other words, your superiors would order you to fire at an unseen location. Or to put it this way, your superiors, your brigade command or your battalion command, would give you orders to fire at locations which the mortar unit itself could not see. So I am asking: What would be the point of repeatedly telling the mortar unit not to target civilians?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: It means not to fire at any other target except those marked as war objectives, or rather, as enemy targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Am I to understand you correctly that your orders were only to fire in circumstances where your side of the conflict was under attack and where it was absolutely necessary to do so?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During the period you were there, September 1992 to September 1993, were there any offensive operations carried out in the north of the city by the corps, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Am I to understand that in that period, your brigade or units of the corps were never involved in any offensive operation to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No, no offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did your brigade have any other mortar or artillery assets apart from your mortar battery?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that really.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I suggest to you that -- or -- withdrawn. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I suggest to you that UNMOs were inhibited in moving around to monitor artillery and mortar units in areas to the north of the city. What would you say about that?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. In the area of our brigade, their movement was never inhibited. It's a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours, Mr. President. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any need to re-examine the witness, Mr. Piletta-Zanin or Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on page 60, line 24, according to what's on my computer, line 24 - thank you - you said that it was never possible to see the mortars by the other side. That is, the mortars are always positioned in such a way that they cannot be seen. My question is the following: And on the other side the mortars of the opponent, were they also hidden in such a way that they could not be seen?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: You're going to have to clarify. Whose mortars? Who couldn't see?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Page 60, line 24 you said that your mortars were positioned in such a way that one could not see them. Now, on the other side, what do you know about that? Those mortars of the other side, were they positioned in the same way, that is, that they could never been seen or else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could first ask clarification as to what the answer of the witness was. Because -- I'll read to the witness what the question and what his answer was. The question to you was -- Mr. Stamp said, "Yes. I'm just understanding you now. While you were at that location --" and you were referring to the location where you were in the winter of 1992/1993 -- "and that is where your mortar unit was positioned, could you see into the part of the city which was under the control of the opposing side?" Your answer then was, "No. The mortars are positioned so that they cannot be seen by the opposing side." Did you then refer to the mortars of the opposing side, that is, the BiH forces, or did you refer to the mortars of the -- on the Serbian side, that could not be seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We couldn't see their mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The positions of their mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think this clarifies it, the answer of the witness in that respect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: A little further on you indicated that you received in your orders the map coordinates of your military targets. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is the following: These coordinates, in general, to what type of facility did they correspond? When we are speaking about -- not about the line in the strictest sense. But when you're talking about military targets scattered in the city, and more particularly, were these targets on upper floors and so on? What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That again is putting words into the witness's mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just opening the door, Mr. President. I'm just opening the door. I'd like to know whether these coordinates corresponded to what kind of facilities. I am not leading. At least, I don't think I'm leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you're not only opening the door, but you're even suggesting what would be behind the door. Did you ever receive any information as to the target at what level at the grid positions given to you, whether this would be ground level or any other level, or was no distinction made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our targets were mortar positions that are located on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, since you spoke of the targets on ground level. When these targets are to be hit by an indirect hit, what is militarily speaking the technique that has to be used, that has to be followed in order to achieve this objective?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I object. The military technique in firing mortars was never enquired to in chief -- in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if the witness takes off his headphones and if his screen is off, then I can respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... And could -- Madam Usher, could you take care that the screen is not on the transcript. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. President, this stems very clearly from the cross-examination. Why is that? Because the Prosecution asked what happened with the coordinates that were transmitted by the command. Now, the thesis of the Prosecution is to say in any case you had the coordinates; therefore, you couldn't make a mistake since you had the coordinates. But we are saying that there are always possibilities to make a mistake, whether you have coordinates or not, and that's linked to various factors. And what I would like to know is whether these people who had the coordinates and who were supposed to fire in reality to those coordinates -- however, they were faced with the possibilities of errors, and this could have caused involuntary damages, and this could have stemmed from the coordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp. But -- you speak English, Mr. Stamp. That's -- let's -- let's just -- I will allow the Defence to put the question to the witness. It has done so, so I will allow the witness to answer that question. But I don't know whether the Chamber could follow your full gymnastic exercise to come to the point -- yes. That's a very friendly translation of what I said. Yes. Could the witness please put his headphones on again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Unfortunately, I am not really good in gymnastics --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, with pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, what can you tell us, please, about the relationship that could exist between the fact that you can have precise coordinates on a map and the getting to the target, that is, the reality of reaching the target in war circumstances, in a war situation? Did you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Theoretically speaking, the first four projectiles, they would go towards the target. They would have to go within 50 metres of the target. While, the fifth projectile should hit the target directly. But once you fire around the target, practically speaking you are more or less hitting the target. But all this is very relative, especially when we're speaking about a mortar projectile. A lot depends on weather conditions, whether there's wind, whether there's no wind. Particularly in Sarajevo, it is a very specific situation because it's a valley. It's a ravine. So if you fire a projectile, you have one set of conditions at the firing position and then on the other side where the projectile is supposed to go. Particularly, the humidity and all other conditions and all that can have an impact on where the projectile will actually land.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. I'm going to come back to other questions that were raised by the Prosecution, on page 64 and from then on, which is in relation to the famous mobile mortars. First question, witness: First of all, as a general rule, the defenders of your lines, were they in a position to specifically see these mobile mortars when they were firing?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: From certain positions our front line was able to see that area where they moved about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You personally? You personally, from your positions, from your mortar positions, were you able to see when they were firing; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, when these mortars are used, at the moment when the firing happens, is the firing done from a static position or is it done from a mobile position?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The vehicle is stationary when it is firing, and then it flees, and then it goes away, it moves away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, in this respect, at the moment of the firing, is there no difference in a sense of mobile nature of one "normal mortar," and the immobile mortar? Is there a difference between a mobile mortar and a normal mortar?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: In the system of firing, there is no difference at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. When the fire is opened from a battery of mortars, no matter what they are, does this ask for a response logically speaking, from a point of view of military technique? And if so, which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I cannot -- perhaps I could be advised, see how that arises again. If there are restrictions on re-examination, I think counsel should abide by those restrictions. There is always a danger that counsel uses re-examination to open new areas, and we are deprived from exploring those new areas. It goes without any check or balance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, your question is about firing from mortars in general, not mobile or immobile, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have two interpretations. I didn't hear anything. I'm sorry. Could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your question was about firing from mortars in general, mobile, immobile. How does this arise from cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yes. I would like to respond, but could, please, we have the same exercise with the witness, if he can take off his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you take your headphones off, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. President, it's very simple. The Prosecution wanted to say earlier or to get the witness to say that this was nonsense to fire at a mobile target such as mortar -- mobile mortars from the point of view of military technique. Now, what I would like to witness to say, if this is the truth, is the following: A mobile mortar is only firing when stationary. When he opens fire and when you cannot see it, which is the case, he cannot be distinguished from any other normal battery, mortar battery. So a normal reflex would be to respond with fire. So that, of course, would be -- we can see what the danger would be of such a mortar. And this is the link between mobile and immobile, and that is the two types of mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may respond to the question. Could you please put your headphones on. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, when a battery fire is opened, whether -- no matter what kind of mortar is in use, what kind of response is invited by the opponent?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The equivalent, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: How do you know that this response has a name -- do you know if there is a special name by which we call this?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. You have been asked a lot of questions about the coordinates, the targets, et cetera. I would like you to make the following exercise: Let's suppose that you are in the field with your unit waiting -- waiting, just waiting, for an order. How do you get the order?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I said at first the orders came by radio station and later on we would have a telephone. The telephone would ring, and then the order would be transmitted by someone from the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: How is the order? What do you get in that order? Do you get the target, the grid references? What do you get?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: If it is about a firing point that we have marked in, then the order would be: Open fire according to the firing point, say, number 3, with three or four projectiles, depending on the need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: So the order includes the number of shells. If it is a different target -- let's suppose that you receive an order to fire to a different place -- what do you do?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Usually such orders are not issued verbally, that is, on the phone. But somebody would come and show us on the map what the target was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: There were some orders in that sense.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In case if there is an offensive or an attack, when their forces would attack, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Once you received the order, what do you have to do? Let's suppose that your last target was target 3 and then you receive the order to target point number 4. What do you have to do?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Then what is done is that the mortar is adjusted according to the angle and the direction. The targeting -- the sight has to be adjusted. I cannot explain it now -- to correspond to the numbers that would correspond to the coordinates, and then that's how you actually directed the mortar according to the distance and the direction into which you want to fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Which is the possibility of making mistakes in that case?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: There is some but there exists -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer. The interpreters didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the probability is, but it exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Were the mortars of your unit moved from time to time?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: They were not moved, and that's primarily because they never managed to locate our positions. If they had managed to locate our position, then we would have been forced to move our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: So from time to time the mortars were moved, weren't they? No?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. What I said: If they had managed to locate us, to find us, then we would have been forced. I said "if." That means they did not manage to find us, to locate us. So we didn't move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: How many charges did you use when firing? Do you know what is a charge?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I do. Of course I do know. It depends on the target. It depends on the distance of the target and our positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Where were you on Christmas Eve 1992? I mean on the 24th of December, Catholic Christmas Eve. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't recall. That was 11 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: New Year's Eve 1992/1993?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the international New Year's -- I mean, 31st? I celebrated New Year's with my friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Orthodox Christmas Eve, on the 7th January 1993?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The house of my grandmother, where I lived with my mother at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi also has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Witness, please, I'd like to ask you briefly perhaps two brief questions. The first question: Do you know about the idea or the reason behind the choice of your position, in terms of tactics -- did you know why -- why did your unit choose -- or your commander, why did he choose this position where you were to be your position and why? What was your objective in having this position there where you had it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, but I haven't text on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you don't need the text on as such, but of course we could ask the usher to ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need it because I don't know how my words are being interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But Judge El Mahdi is speaking French, and we are listening to his French. So it's only for the Prosecution that receives interpretation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The position was chosen because it was located on the side of the hill which cannot be seen from the positions under the control of the Muslim forces. And it's on the other slope, opposite slope, which is an ideal position. It is the hardest possible position for those who are targeting it. So when a mortar projectile fires, it falls at the same angle under which it is fired. So because then the opposite side would not be -- so that's the reason why the mortars were precisely located there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You said that you were never the target by the other side because the opposing side never managed to locate your position, and you added that that was normal, that if at any point the opposing side would have found the mortar position, then this position would have to change. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: They could suppose where the position was, but they could never hit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes. But I'm thinking of something else. You did locate the location where the mortars of the opposing side were, and you said that those positions were targeted, fired on, by your unit. However, if they had stayed where they were, would your firing, would it hit their targets and that's the reason why you said in answering the Judge Nieto-Navia that it could happen that you were firing on the same positions one or more times? And I'm talking about the opposing side's position. So following your logic, from the moment when the opposing side felt that it was uncovered, that it was found, that it was located, they would change positions. So now I understand that what you're saying is that the opposing side, however, stayed put. So do you think that they were -- did you hit them? Do you believe that you hit them with your mortar fire or that you didn't, that you missed your target and that's the reason why you had to repeat your attacks? What I mean is: What is your explanation? I cannot follow what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: When I was talking about the position of their mortars, I said "in the area." And when I'm saying "area," that means a wider space. They probably could move -- they moved within that space, within that area. When there is a response -- a firing response of a mortar, if they again hit, they will get hit from the same distance so that they think -- so that they make you think that you didn't discover their positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But you are saying that you targeted them and you fired at predetermined positions where there were mortars. Now, my question is simply: After your fires, two things could happen. Either such a mortar has been destroyed or it hasn't been hit. In either case, how does a position which has already been identified by the adverse party continues there, continues in that same position, continues in the same place? I don't know whether my question is clear, or do you want me to reword it.

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Try to understand what I'm saying, that is, the tactics to fire from the same place again, if we return the fire. So that we would think that we had missed. That is, they fire from the same place so that we would think that we had missed and that we would stop thinking that that was the target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean you believe that you did hit the mortars which were there and that they were bringing other mortars but always to the same place? Is that it? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SASA KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: We were trying to hit them. Whether they brought in other mortars, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have a few questions for you as well, but it would take too much time to do that today. And there is a chance that one of the parties would put subsequently questions to you as well. Therefore, I would -- I would like to tell you that we have to continue tomorrow in the afternoon. It will not be for a very long time. I take that it will not be more than 10, 15, perhaps 20 minutes. I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony as you have given it until now in this courtroom or you're still about to give tomorrow. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is the issue you wanted to raise to be dealt with in the presence of the witness or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I'm very sorry, but I think simply, unfortunately, I will be absent from here for extra reasons, and one question which I wanted to ask and which arose from Judge El Mahdi's questions. I do not know whether I'm allowed to do it now. This is merely a clarification. Or should I pass -- transmit my message to Mrs. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to wait until tomorrow as well, so the Defence also, unfortunately, has to wait until tomorrow and then can see whether there are any further questions arising out of the questions of the Bench. So if you would please pass that to Mrs. Pilipovic, then she certainly will take care of that. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom. Meanwhile, I'll inform the parties that Ms. Tournaye is available for a meeting tomorrow at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until tomorrow, same courtroom, quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
